cards.title: Constant lifetime recourse for competitive online matching on the line
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic online algorithm A and absolute constants α≥1 and B∈N such that A maintains an α-competitive minimum-cost matching on the line while reassigning every individual request at most B times over its entire lifetime? For every finite known set S of labeled servers with real locations, and every sequence r₁,…,rₙ of requests with real locations, n≤|S|, A must after each arrival t output an injection M_t:{r₁,…,r_t}→S. Require Σ_{i≤t}|rᵢ−M_t(rᵢ)|≤α OPT_t at every t, and for each i require |{t:i<t≤n and M_t(rᵢ)≠M_{t−1}(rᵢ)}|≤B. Here OPT_t is the minimum cost of an injection of the first t requests into S. The constants and the algorithm are independent of n, the locations, their spread and the arrival order.
cards.why: Would determine whether online uncertainty in a basic geometric assignment problem can be absorbed by only a bounded number of revisions to each individual decision.

cards.definitions: A server or request has an identity and a location on the real line; expressions inside absolute values denote locations. Every request can use every server, with edge cost their distance. As in the source’s positive-cost model, request–server distances are positive; no lower bound on them or on the ratio of largest to smallest distance is promised. All server locations are revealed before the first request. A new request reveals only itself; future requests are unknown, and the algorithm must finish its update before the next one arrives. At most one request occupies a server. Previously matched requests may be assigned to different servers during an update, with simultaneous replacement of the matching permitted. The first assignment of a new request is not a reassignment. The displayed lifetime count concerns changes between maintained matchings and excludes internal auxiliary computations. It bounds each request separately, not just the sum divided by n, and it does not impose a constant limit on how many different requests can move at a single arrival. Competitive cost is the total length of the current matching, with no additive term and no sum over previous matching costs. Determinism follows the model of the source’s exhibited algorithms and is made explicit as an editorial convention; randomized expected guarantees constitute a separate extension. The target restricts recourse and competitive ratio, not update running time; a uniform algorithm may perform finite exact arithmetic and comparisons on revealed real coordinates.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one online algorithm with universal constants α,B satisfying both inequalities for every instance and every prefix, or prove that no such deterministic algorithm and constants exist. A constant bound only on average reassignments, a bound per arrival without control of each request’s lifetime, or a guarantee only for alternating instances is not the stated result. An impossibility result must cover all deterministic algorithms in this model, not just the source’s algorithm.

context_blocks.title: A stronger requirement than amortized recourse
context_blocks.text: The source obtains a constant competitive ratio with O(log n) average reassignments per request. This controls the total number of changes; it need not keep any particular request from moving many times. Its second concluding question asks whether a constant number per request can suffice, as in its alternating-instance result. The first concluding question, about recourse available per iteration, is distinct.

context_blocks.title: The alternating case gives the lifetime interpretation
context_blocks.text: An instance is alternating when there is a server between any two request locations. The 2025 journal version gives a (1+ε)-competitive algorithm in this special case that reassigns each request O(1/ε²) times, and explicitly leaves constant recourse for general instances open. This per-request lifetime guarantee supplies the interpretation used in the statement.

context_blocks.title: The journal tradeoff does not give both constants
context_blocks.text: For 1≤f(n)≤log n, the journal version gives competitive ratio O(f(n)) with amortized recourse O(log n/f(n)). Taking f constant retains logarithmic amortized recourse; taking f logarithmic retains a logarithmic competitive ratio. The theorem therefore does not provide simultaneous constant competitiveness and constant lifetime recourse.

context_blocks.title: A 2026 stability lower bound uses a different arrival model
context_blocks.text: De Berg, Schmidt-Kraepelin and Ștef prove that sublogarithmic per-update stability cannot maintain a bounded approximation in their matching model. Even its bipartite version inserts a server and a client together. It is not the present model with all servers known initially, and its per-update cost is different from a lifetime bound for each request.

cards.title: Communication lower bounds for interactive pure-private shuffled summation
cards.formal: What lower bound on worst-case per-user communication is necessary for interactive pure ε-differentially private binary summation in the shuffle model? There are n users with bits x₁,…,xₙ, and an analyst estimates s(x)=Σᵢxᵢ. The antecedent is the source’s noninteractive lower bound Ω_{ε,χ}(√log n) bits per user for expected absolute error at most n^{1/2−χ}, with fixed ε>0 and χ>0; in particular it rules out constant communication at error bounded independently of n. The source asks whether any nontrivial communication lower bound persists with interaction. Its interaction rules and the requested strength of the bound remain unspecified, so this is not yet a single complete asymptotic target.
cards.why: Would clarify whether adaptive anonymous communication can avoid the communication overhead of accurate pure-private aggregation, and which limitations come from privacy versus the one-round restriction.
cards.status_note: Read the original conference and full-version communication statements and concluding question, plus the 2024 paper’s main theorem and open questions. Later-work searches through 12 September 2026 found no result settling a specified general interactive version. The main obstacle to certification here is the source’s missing interactive model and lower-bound threshold.

sentences: Each user holds one bit and an analyst must estimate the sum from anonymous messages.
Pure differential privacy protects the entire transcript when one user’s bit changes.
The original lower bound concerns worst-case bits per user in noninteractive protocols with sub-square-root expected absolute error.
The question asks for a communication lower bound that also permits interaction.
The interactive model and the strength of a nontrivial bound must still be fixed; later bounds on expected communication do not resolve those choices.

cards.definitions: A noninteractive shuffle protocol consists of a local randomized encoder, independently applied to each user’s bit, a trusted shuffler that uniformly permutes the resulting messages and removes sender identities, and an analyst that estimates the sum from the shuffled messages. Multiple messages from one user are allowed. For a complete analyst-visible transcript T, pure ε differential privacy requires Pr[T(x)∈E]≤exp(ε)Pr[T(x′)∈E] for every measurable event E and all x,x′∈{0,1}ⁿ differing in one coordinate. Probabilities include all protocol randomness; there is no additive δ allowance. Privacy must hold for the exposed transcript, not merely the final estimate. Expected absolute error at most a(n) means sup_x E[|ŝ−s(x)|]≤a(n). The source’s communication cost is a worst-case bound on the number of bits a user sends, including all its messages; for a fixed m-message encoder over a k-symbol alphabet the natural bit representation costs m⌈log₂k⌉. Expected message counts are a different resource. In the contemplated extension, later messages may depend on earlier communication, but the cited question does not define the permitted dependencies or what information survives each shuffle. Constants in the displayed lower bound may depend on fixed privacy and error-exponent parameters but not on n.
cards.answer_criterion: After the missing protocol class and quantitative target are fixed, establish the required communication lower bound for every protocol in that class, with privacy and accuracy exactly as stated, or refute that particular bound by a protocol satisfying those conditions. A noninteractive lower bound alone, a local-model lower bound, or an expected-communication guarantee does not establish a worst-case lower bound with interaction. The present source question has no fully specified acceptance threshold.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
